fatal_errors: The proposed Q235/native-oxide system does not reconstruct the target system of an AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coating deposited on SS316L by atmospheric plasma spraying and subsequently annealed.
The intervention omits the defining coating process, 150 µm coating thickness, feedstock characteristics, and the 400–850 °C annealing comparison with a 550 °C optimum.
The exposure conditions do not match either the target 3.5 wt% H2SO4 electrochemical test or the 900 °C cyclic Na2SO4/NaCl/V2O5 hot-corrosion tests.
No prior evidence is cited, and the assertion that native oxide on Q235 remains passivating in chloride-rich aqueous media is not adequately justified.

The falsification rule tests whether thermal conditioning improves corrosion resistance, not whether temperature-induced native-film destabilization is the governing cause; therefore, a null treatment effect would not decisively falsify the stated mechanism.
explanation: The response presents a generic, testable alternative concerning thermal modification of native iron oxide on Q235, but it has little scientific agreement with the hidden target. The only mechanistic overlap is the broad idea that oxide-film integrity can suppress corrosion and that defects permit localized attack. It misses the HEA coating, APS deposition, annealing-temperature series, BCC/FCC and grain-refinement mediators, Al/Cr-rich passive products, and all quantitative corrosion conditions and outcomes. Its experiment includes an untreated reference and useful surface and mass-loss measurements, but the thermal treatment is unspecified and lacks sham or oxide-removal controls, electrochemical measurements, and direct defect/adherence quantification. Most importantly, comparing conditioned and untreated specimens cannot distinguish oxide composition, roughness, residual stress, and heat-induced substrate changes, and the proposed null result does not directly test the claimed temperature dependence. With no supporting evidence and several unsubstantiated assumptions, this is not a well-supported plausible alternative.
